consensus_summary: All four blind responses identify the ship primarily as the Church — the vessel of salvation (the 'Barque of Peter,' typologically Noah's ark) carrying believers safely through the sea of the world toward salvation, grounded in the Gospel storm narratives, Luke 5, Genesis 6–9, and 1 Peter 3:20–21. Secondary meanings listed include the individual life/soul's voyage, worldly commerce and pride (ships of Tarshish, Tyre, Babylon), Jonah's flight, and Christ himself as vessel.
book_summary: The book identifies the ship as an earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding upon the sea of peoples: rulers as pilots, inhabitants as crew, armies as defenders, wealth as cargo. It explicitly denies the ecclesial reading's logic — Christ needs no constructed vessel beneath him, walking on the sea directly; when he boards a ship it is a body brought under its true Head. The ship may be broken while its people survive (Acts 27).
consensus_core_identification: Ship = the Church, the corporate vessel of salvation bearing believers through the world toward safety.
book_core_identification: Ship = an earthly kingdom, city, or governed political body (e.g., Tyre, Babylon) sailing upon the sea of peoples — expressly not a vessel Christ requires or identifies with the Church.
boundary_disagreement: The book elevates what the consensus treats as a secondary, context-specific meaning (ships as commerce, pride, and worldly power in Ezek 27, Isa 23, Rev 18) into the primary and defining identification, while stripping the Gospel boat scenes and Noah's ark of their ecclesial referent. Gospel boats are reinterpreted as human political/constructed bodies brought under Christ's headship rather than the Church itself; Acts 27 becomes an emblem of a state broken while its people survive, not the Church preserved.
material_contradiction: The consensus says the ship is the Church, the divinely appointed vessel of salvation; the book says the ship is an earthly polity and pointedly notes that Christ needs no constructed body beneath him — he walks on the sea directly. Both cannot be true of the same symbol in the same sense: accepting the book requires rejecting the ecclesial identification as the primary referent, and the book's common-view note flags 'the Church' precisely as the commonly taught view it departs from.
rationale: All four consensus responses converge on ship = Church as the settled primary meaning. The book replaces this central referent with 'earthly kingdom/city/political body,' a reading related to but broader and more institutional than the consensus's 'commerce/wealth/pride' alternative (which was framed as economic imagery, not the identification of the ship with a governed polity as such). The book's rhetorical move — Christ walking on the sea without a vessel, the ship as merely a human construction under its true Head — directly undercuts the ecclesial reading rather than refining its boundary. Some extension overlaps (Tyre, Babylon, Acts 27 appear in consensus alternatives), but the center is replaced, so DIVERGENT rather than REFINED.
strongest_objection: The consensus responses already list ships as symbols of worldly commerce, wealth, and the political-commercial power of Tyre and Babylon (Ezek 27, Isa 23 territory, Rev 18) as a 'common' alternative; one could argue the book merely promotes an acknowledged alternative to primary status, which might be read as REFINED rather than DIVERGENT. However, the book does more than reweight: it identifies the ship as the political body itself (not merely its commerce) and explicitly negates the ecclesial reading's premise, which is replacement of the central referent, not boundary adjustment.
